catalog_quote: Sri Lanka Malay words do not show different levels of prominence in their syllables, neither phonologically nor phonetically. In other words, there is no word accent or stress. Smith et al. (2004) claim that “stress falls on the long vowel of a word, or on the initial syllable if the word only contains only short vowels.” They do not state by which acoustic cue they established the location of stress, so that we are probably dealing with an impressionistic statement here. Bakker (2006) reports accent on the first syllable, drawing on Robuchon (2003). These statements again seem to be impressionistic. Some instrumental analyses were undertaken to check these claims, but no cues for a saliently prominent (stressed) syllable could be found. 49 words with different syllable structures were checked in 6 different controlled environments with two male native speakers of SLM for pitch contour …
sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title (Apoussidou & Nordhoff 2008, OCP5 Toulouse talk): existence verified on the archived OCP5 programme (Fri 25 Jan 2008, 15h00), but no abstract, handout or slides exist anywhere open (booklet never posted; author pages, Crossref, LingBuzz, OpenAlex/S2, Scholar, Bing all empty or blocked; session was already exhausted). Its findings are reported first-hand by the same authors in the catalog's deciding source, Nordhoff 2009 (LOT 226), which was downloaded from LOT and read: catalog quote verified verbatim at sec. 4.4.5 p. 117; instrumental study finds no pitch/intensity prominence cue, duration and vowel quality rejected as stress cues, vowel length analysed by extrametricality + bimoraic foot (sec. 4.5), SLM framed as stressless like its Malayic/Javanese input languages (sec. 4.5.4). catalog's classification no word stress confirmed; nothing supersedes Nordhoff 2009.

new_statements.reading: Sri Lanka Malay has no word stress or accent: the author's own instrumental study (with Apoussidou; 49 words, 6 environments, 2 male speakers) finds no pitch or intensity cue of prominence; duration is rejected as a cue (long vowels are explained instead by final-syllable extrametricality plus a bimoraic-foot requirement, sec. 4.5), and vowel quality only marks the root antepenult as non-prominent without picking out a prominent syllable (p. 120). Earlier impressionistic claims (Smith et al. 2004: stress on the long vowel, else initial; Bakker 2006 / Robuchon 2003: initial accent) are explicitly rejected. This is the catalog's existing deciding source; the quote is verified verbatim at p. 117.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened via its extracted text text (lines 5601-5621). new_statements.relation_note: As far as it goes (title only), the work agrees with the catalog's existing statement that Sri Lanka Malay has no word stress; Nordhoff 2009 (the catalog's deciding source, held by the project) cites this very talk twice on p. 117 as the instrumental study behind that statement. The talk adds nothing citable beyond Nordhoff 2009; it should be treated as unpublished/unobtainable rather than as an independent deciding source.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The open copy is only the conference programme: it gives the talk's title ('no stress, please!') and slot, no abstract or body text. The title alone asserts that Sri Lanka Malay has no stress, but the work's own statement of the evidence is not in any open copy. The abstract booklet page archived by the the Internet Archive on 2008-12-25 reads only 'Abstract Booklet for OCP5 / COMING SOON..', and the the Internet Archive's index listing for w3.erss.univ-tlse2.fr/OCP5/* (7 captures: index, abstract_booklet.htm, committees.htm, travel.htm, workshop.htm) shows / were never captured. The talk's content is reported first-hand only in Nordhoff 2009 (already held by the project), sec. 4.4.5 p. 117: '49 words with different syllable structures were checked in 6 different controlled environments with two male native speakers of SLM for pitch contour and intensity. The compiled measurements taken together do not suggest that a meaningful generalization about the correlation between word structure and pitch or intensity can be made (Apoussidou & Nordhoff 2008).' Bibliography entry p. 714: 'Apoussidou, D. & S. Nordhoff (2008). "Feet in Sri Lanka Malay – no stress please". Paper presented at OCP 5, January 2008, Toulouse.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in any open copy of this work.
new_statements.exceptions: None available; no text of the talk is open.
new_statements.identity_note: Nordhoff 2009 describes Upcountry Sri Lanka Malay (Kandy area); the OCP5 talk (same authors' instrumental data, 2 male speakers) is the study reported there. No other variety is described in the material opened.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated locators in the open-access PDF we hold of Nordhoff 2009 (811-pp reference grammar, LOT 226), which is the sole full grammar in Glottolog's list and bases its 'no word stress' classification on the author's own acoustic measurements (with Apoussidou), explicitly weighing and rejecting the earlier impressionistic stress claims. Crossref/Glottolog checks found no later or competing instrumental/phonological study of SLM stress (the OCP5 talk was never published; no JIPA Illustration; the 2013 Brill chapter is a same-author sketch, not OA).1 bib held locally.
